title: Common Sense and The American Crisis
author: Thomas Paine
setting: Philadelphia and the American War of Independence, from the retreat across New Jersey in 1776 to the peace of 1783
lengthNote: Common Sense runs to about 21,000 words: an introduction, four sections, an Appendix and an address to the Quakers. The American Crisis is sixteen papers written between December 1776 and December 1783, from about 1,200 words (No. IV) to more than 12,000 (No. III)
openingLine: Perhaps the sentiments contained in the following pages, are not yet sufficiently fashionable to procure them general favor;
summary: Thomas Paine landed in Philadelphia from England at the end of 1774, and just over a year later he published the pamphlet that argued Americans out of their loyalty to the king. Common Sense, which appeared without its author’s name in January 1776, says that society is a blessing and government at best a necessary evil, that monarchy and hereditary succession are absurd, that an island cannot govern a continent, and that the time for independence has come. The enlarged edition of February adds an Appendix, answering the king’s latest speech, and an address to the Quaker leaders who had declared for the Crown. The American Crisis begins in December 1776, during the retreat across New Jersey, with “These are the times that try men’s souls”, and follows the war in sixteen papers: open letters to British generals, commissioners and ministers and to the people of England, calls for courage and for taxes, and, in April 1783, a farewell announcing that the times that tried men’s souls are over.
referenceStyle: section for Common Sense (Introduction; Of the Origin and Design of Government; Of Monarchy and Hereditary Succession; Thoughts on the Present State of American Affairs; Of the Present Ability of America; Appendix; To the Quakers) and number for The American Crisis (Crisis I to XIII, the Crisis Extraordinary and the two Supernumerary papers)

sourceText.label: Common Sense, Project Gutenberg eBook 147, a transcription of the enlarged Bradford edition (Philadelphia, 14 February 1776); The American Crisis, from The Writings of Thomas Paine, vol. 1, ed. Moncure Daniel Conway (1894), Project Gutenberg eBook 3741
sourceText.note: The Common Sense quotations have been checked against a scan of the Bradford printing and keep its spelling and capitals, such as independance. Gutenberg’s text refers the reader to page forty for the Continental Charter, where the 1776 printings consulted say twenty-five or fifty-four. Conway prints the Crisis papers in Paine’s own numbering, thirteen numbered papers with the Crisis Extraordinary and the two Supernumerary papers, and his spelling is lightly modernised.

structure.label: Common Sense: Introduction; Of the Origin and Design of Government
structure.title: Society, government and the English constitution
structure.summary: Paine opens by warning that a long habit of not thinking a thing wrong gives it a superficial appearance of being right, and declares that the cause of America is in a great measure the cause of all mankind. The first section separates society, produced by our wants, from government, produced by our wickedness, and imagines a few settlers meeting under a tree to make their first laws, then choosing representatives as their numbers grow. Against this simple model he sets the celebrated English constitution of king, lords and commons, which he calls the base remains of two ancient tyrannies mixed with some new republican materials, and in which the crown, as the giver of places and pensions, always has its way.

scenes.title: The cause of all mankind
scenes.summary: Custom and reason, and a postscript of 14 February explaining the delay of this edition.

scenes.ref: Of the Origin and Design of Government
scenes.title: A blessing and a necessary evil
scenes.summary: Society from our wants, government from our wickedness, and a colony under a tree.

scenes.ref: Of the Origin and Design of Government
scenes.title: The English constitution
scenes.summary: King, lords and commons, and a door locked against absolute monarchy with the key given to the crown.

structure.label: Common Sense: Of Monarchy and Hereditary Succession
structure.title: Kings and their heirs
structure.summary: Mankind were originally equals, Paine argues, and while differences of wealth can be explained, the distinction of kings and subjects has no natural or religious reason. He goes to scripture: for nearly three thousand years from the creation the Jews had no king, Gideon refused a crown, and Samuel warned the people what a king would take from them. Hereditary succession is worse still, an insult to posterity that nature mocks by giving mankind an ass for a lion. The first king of the present English line was a French bastard landing with an armed banditti, and far from preventing civil wars, succession has brought England eight civil wars and nineteen rebellions since the Conquest.

scenes.title: Gideon and Samuel
scenes.summary: The scriptural case against kings, and monarchy as the Popery of government.

scenes.title: An ass for a lion
scenes.summary: Hereditary right, William the Conqueror, and the wars of York and Lancaster.

structure.label: Common Sense: Thoughts on the Present State of American Affairs
structure.title: The case for separation
structure.summary: Offering nothing more than simple facts, plain arguments and common sense, Paine declares that the period of debate is closed: since the fighting of 19 April 1775, all the old plans for reconciliation are like the almanacs of last year. He answers the case for staying with Britain point by point. America would have flourished without her; Britain protected the colonies for the sake of her own trade; Europe, not England, is the parent country; the connection drags America into European wars; and it is absurd for a continent to be governed by an island. Reconciliation would leave the king a veto over every American law. Paine sketches a continental government, with a large Congress and a Continental Charter, and answers the question where the King of America is: in America the law is king.

scenes.ref: Thoughts on the Present State of American Affairs
scenes.title: The period of debate is closed
scenes.summary: Arms as the last resource, and the seed time of continental union.

scenes.ref: Thoughts on the Present State of American Affairs
scenes.title: Answers to the reconcilers
scenes.summary: Protection, the parent country, Boston, and a continent governed by an island.

scenes.ref: Thoughts on the Present State of American Affairs
scenes.title: A continental charter
scenes.summary: Annual assemblies, a Congress of at least 390, and a crown broken up and scattered among the people.

structure.label: Common Sense: Of the Present Ability of America; Appendix; To the Quakers
structure.title: Strength, the Appendix and the Quakers
structure.summary: The last section argues that America is strong enough now: its numbers suit its needs, it has no debt, and it has the timber, tar, iron and hemp to build a navy, whose cost the enlarged edition calculates ship by ship from British figures. Youth is the seed time of good habits, and the time to form a government is before interests divide. The Appendix answers the king’s speech, which reached Philadelphia on the day the pamphlet first appeared, and ends with the birthday of a new world. The address to the Quakers tells the authors of their Ancient Testimony that bearing arms in defence is less sinful than making war, and that in declaring for the king they have mixed religion with politics.

scenes.ref: Of the Present Ability of America
scenes.title: A fleet and a union
scenes.summary: Numbers, debt, timber, and a navy costed rate by rate.

scenes.title: The king’s speech
scenes.summary: The speech that arrived with the first edition, and the birthday of a new world.

scenes.title: The Ancient Testimony
scenes.summary: A reply to the Quaker leaders who declared for the king.

structure.label: The American Crisis I–IV (December 1776 to September 1777)
structure.title: The retreat, Trenton and the Brandywine
structure.summary: Paine began the first Crisis at Newark during the retreat across New Jersey, and it appeared in the Pennsylvania Journal on 19 December 1776, a week before Washington crossed the Delaware to attack Trenton. It opens with “These are the times that try men’s souls”, describes the retreat from Fort Lee, praises Washington’s fortitude, and tells of a Tory tavern-keeper who wanted peace in his day. The second paper, addressed to Lord Howe in January 1777, mocks his proclamation offering pardons; the third, dated on the second anniversary of Lexington, reviews the whole quarrel and sets out the case for independence under four heads; the fourth was written the day after the defeat at the Brandywine.

scenes.title: The times that try men’s souls
scenes.summary: The retreat to the Delaware, and a call to every state.

scenes.title: To Lord Howe
scenes.summary: A proclamation answered by a Crisis.

scenes.title: A review of the quarrel
scenes.summary: Four reasons for independence, and a test for the disaffected.

scenes.title: After the Brandywine
scenes.summary: A defeat treated as a check, and a warning to Howe.

structure.label: The American Crisis V–VIII (March 1778 to March 1780)
structure.title: Howe, the commissioners and the people of England
structure.summary: Written at Lancaster in March 1778, with the British in Philadelphia, the fifth paper mocks Sir William Howe with a design for his monument, then turns to the inhabitants of America with a plan for filling the army. The sixth answers the peace commissioners of 1778, the Earl of Carlisle, General Clinton and William Eden, whose cargo of pardons will have no market and whose manifesto threatens that the whole contest is changed. The seventh and eighth are addressed to the people of England: war can never be the interest of a trading nation, and the English, safe on their island, have known nothing of the war but its taxes.

scenes.title: To General Sir William Howe
scenes.summary: A monument for the knight of the windmill, and an address to America.

scenes.title: To the commissioners
scenes.summary: Pardons that have become a perfect drug, and a threat returned.

scenes.title: To the people of England
scenes.summary: A trading nation at war with its own customers.

scenes.title: Address to the people of England
scenes.summary: Fleets in the Channel, and a war known only by its taxes.

structure.label: The American Crisis IX–XI, the Crisis Extraordinary and the first Supernumerary Crisis (June 1780 to May 1782)
structure.title: Charleston, taxes and Yorktown
structure.summary: The ninth paper, of June 1780, treats the loss of Charleston as a call to wake up: America ever is what she thinks herself to be. The Crisis Extraordinary, in October, sets the taxes of England against the sum needed to defend America and argues that conquest would multiply the burden. After the surrender of Cornwallis at Yorktown, the tenth paper answers the king’s speech and asks the states to pay the quotas Congress has set; the eleventh warns that Britain is trying to separate America from France; and a Supernumerary Crisis of May 1782 asks Sir Guy Carleton to give up the loyalist who hanged Captain Huddy of the New Jersey militia, so that Captain Asgill, the British officer chosen by lot for retaliation, need not die.

scenes.title: The loss of Charleston
scenes.summary: A defeat that rouses a sleeping country.

scenes.title: On the subject of taxation
scenes.summary: Forty shillings a head in England against thirteen and fourpence in America.

scenes.title: On the king’s speech
scenes.summary: Cornwallis, Silas Deane, and the quotas of eight million dollars.

scenes.ref: Crisis XI; Supernumerary Crisis (To Sir Guy Carleton)
scenes.title: News and a hanging
scenes.summary: No separate peace, and the case of Huddy and Asgill.

structure.label: The American Crisis XII, XIII and the last Supernumerary Crisis (October 1782 to December 1783)
structure.title: Peace and the union
structure.summary: The twelfth paper answers the Earl of Shelburne, Britain’s first minister, who had said that the sun of England’s glory would set when Parliament acknowledged American independence. The thirteenth, published on 19 April 1783, the eighth anniversary of Lexington, opens with “The times that tried men’s souls are over” and turns to what peace demands: a good national character, which Paine rates as highly as independence, and above all the union of the states, since the world knows Americans by no other title. The last paper, sent from New York in December 1783, attacks Lord Sheffield’s plan to keep the West India carrying trade in British ships and argues that only a union able to act on commerce can answer it.

scenes.title: To the Earl of Shelburne
scenes.summary: The sun of England’s glory, and a giant and a dwarf.

scenes.title: Thoughts on the peace
scenes.summary: The times that tried men’s souls are over; our great title is Americans.

scenes.ref: Supernumerary Crisis (To the People of America)
scenes.title: The carrying trade
scenes.summary: Lord Sheffield’s pamphlet, and a union with power over commerce.

characters.name: Thomas Paine
characters.role: The author, who signed his papers Common Sense
characters.summary: An English staymaker and dismissed excise officer from Thetford, Paine arrived in Philadelphia at the end of 1774 with a letter from Benjamin Franklin, edited a magazine, and published Common Sense anonymously in January 1776. He served as a volunteer aide to General Nathanael Greene during the retreat of 1776, became secretary to the Congress’s Committee for Foreign Affairs, lost the post in the quarrel over Silas Deane, and went to France in 1781 to help raise money. He took no profit from Common Sense, and signed every Crisis paper with its title.
characters.clue: A former excise officer from Thetford, he began a paper at Newark on the retreat and signed it with the title of his first pamphlet.

characters.name: George III
characters.summary: Never named in Common Sense, the king is its real target: the hardened, sullen-tempered Pharaoh of England who can hear of his subjects’ slaughter and sleep, and the Royal Brute of Britain, whose speech to Parliament reached Philadelphia on the day the pamphlet first appeared. In the first Crisis he is the sottish, stupid, stubborn, worthless, brutish man to whom Paine will never swear allegiance, and his speech after Yorktown is answered in the tenth.
characters.clue: Called the Royal Brute of Britain and the sullen-tempered Pharaoh of England, he is the man to whom the writer will never swear allegiance.

characters.name: George Washington
characters.summary: In the first Crisis Paine, who marched with the troops from Fort Lee to the Delaware, compares him to King William, who never appeared to full advantage but in difficulties and in action, and credits him with a mind that can even flourish upon care. According to a tradition repeated by Conway, Washington had the paper read to his soldiers before Trenton. In January 1776 he had written of the sound doctrine and unanswerable reasoning of Common Sense.
characters.clue: Compared with King William, he never appears to full advantage except in difficulties, and has a mind that can even flourish upon care.

characters.name: Benjamin Franklin
characters.summary: Paine knew Franklin in London and came to America with his letter of introduction. In a note to the third Crisis he recalls that in October 1775 Franklin offered him materials for a history of the troubles, and that he had already begun Common Sense and sent Franklin the first copy printed. The pamphlet was at first attributed to Franklin, who wrote in February 1776 that Paine was the reputed and, he thought, the real author.
characters.clue: Suspected at first of writing the pamphlet himself, this patron from London days was sent the first copy printed.

characters.name: Lord Howe
characters.role: Peace commissioner, addressed in the second Crisis
characters.summary: With his brother, General Howe, Lord Howe came to America empowered to offer pardons, and their joint proclamation of 30 November 1776 ordered all congresses and committees to disband. Paine addresses the second Crisis to him, sets his own paper against the proclamation, recalls that America had raised a monument to Howe’s dead brother, and tells him that no messenger was ever sent on a more foolish errand.
characters.clue: His proclamation is answered by a Crisis, and he is told he is a commissioner without authority on the most foolish errand ever sent.

characters.name: Sir William Howe
characters.summary: The general who drives Washington’s army across New Jersey in 1776 and takes Philadelphia in 1777 is Paine’s chief military adversary. Paine says in the first Crisis that Howe’s campaign is rather a ravage than a conquest. In the fifth, written at Lancaster in March 1778, he addresses Howe with extended mockery, looking for a suitable monument for the new knight of the windmill and post.
characters.clue: Newly knighted, he is offered a mock monument as the knight of the windmill and post.

characters.name: Nathanael Greene
characters.summary: The Continental general who commanded the garrison at Fort Lee on 20 November 1776, when the British landed above it and the retreat began. Paine, his volunteer aide-de-camp, describes him (spelled Green in the text) ordering the men under arms and sending an express to Washington at Hackensack.
characters.clue: Commanding the garrison at Fort Lee, he orders the men under arms and sends an express to headquarters at Hackensack.

characters.name: The Tories
characters.summary: For Paine the Tories are Americans who opposed independence and sided with Britain. Common Sense sorts the reconcilers into interested men, weak men, prejudiced men and moderate men, and ends by hoping that the names of Whig and Tory will be extinct. In the Crisis papers the tone hardens: every Tory is a coward, the tavern-keeper at Amboy wants peace in his own day, and Paine proposes tests, taxes and exile for the disaffected.
characters.clue: Interested, weak, prejudiced or merely moderate, they want peace in their own day and are told that servile fear is the foundation of their creed.
characters.firstAppearance: Common Sense, Thoughts on the Present State of American Affairs

characters.name: The Quaker leaders
characters.summary: Paine, whose father was a Quaker, addresses the representatives of the Society of Friends who published The Ancient Testimony early in 1776, which declared that the setting up and putting down of kings is God’s peculiar prerogative and then urged subordination to the king. He tells them they have mistaken party for conscience, and in the second Crisis attacks a further Quaker testimony, signed by John Pemberton in December 1776.
characters.clue: Their Ancient Testimony leaves the setting up and putting down of kings to God, then urges subordination to one.

characters.name: The Carlisle commissioners
characters.summary: The Earl of Carlisle, General Clinton and William Eden were sent in 1778, after the French alliance, with offers of pardon and the repeal of the offending acts. Paine’s sixth Crisis answers their last proclamation, which warned that if America joined France the whole contest was changed, and asks whether they consider themselves men or devils.
characters.clue: Their cargo of pardons will find no market, and they are asked whether they are men or devils.

characters.name: Silas Deane
characters.role: American agent in France, attacked by Paine
characters.summary: A former member of Congress sent to France to obtain supplies. Paine accused him in print of attempting a fraud on the public funds, a quarrel that cost Paine his post as secretary to the Committee for Foreign Affairs in January 1779. In the tenth Crisis Paine says that Deane rose like a rocket and fell like a stick, calls him a plodding, plotting, cringing mercenary who had turned to treason in France, and says his name, like Arnold’s, ought to be forgotten.
characters.clue: He rose like a rocket and fell like a stick, and his name, like Arnold’s, is to be forgotten.

characters.name: Lord Shelburne
characters.summary: The Earl of Shelburne, head of the British ministry that made peace. The twelfth Crisis answers a speech in which he said that whenever Parliament acknowledged American independence the sun of England’s glory would set, and that he wished he could plead before Congress. Paine replies that independence is the only way out of the war and that America cannot be pleaded back into dependence.
characters.clue: He warns that the sun of England’s glory will set with American independence, and wishes he could plead before Congress.

characters.name: Sir Guy Carleton
characters.role: British commander at New York in 1782
characters.summary: In May 1782 Paine addresses a Supernumerary Crisis to the new British commander in New York. Captain Huddy of the New Jersey militia had been taken from prison and hanged by loyalist refugees under a Captain Lippincott, and Captain Asgill of the Guards had been chosen by lot to die in retaliation. Paine asks Carleton to give up the murderer and save his own officer.
characters.clue: He is asked to give up a murderer and so save his own officer, a captain chosen by lot to die for a crime not his own.

characters.name: William the Conqueror
characters.role: Paine’s example of a king’s origins
characters.summary: In Common Sense the Norman Conquest shows how the English crown began: a French bastard landing with an armed banditti and making himself king against the consent of the natives. Paine uses him to prove that the antiquity of English monarchy will not bear looking into, and turns him against the parent-country argument: if descent decided government, England ought to be governed by France.
characters.clue: A French bastard landing with an armed banditti, he founded the present English line and is a very paltry rascally original.
characters.firstAppearance: Common Sense, Of Monarchy and Hereditary Succession

themes.name: Independence
themes.summary: Common Sense makes independence a matter of plain fact: a continent should not be governed by an island three thousand miles away, a colony that has come of age cannot stay a ward, and every argument for reconciliation was answered by the shots of 19 April 1775. Paine insists that independence means only whether Americans shall make their own laws, and in the Crisis papers he defends the Declaration as the sense of the people given a legal form.
themes.development: Now is the seed time of continental union; ’Tis time to part; a continent governed by an island; the independency is ours, not theirs; Our great title is AMERICANS.

themes.name: Monarchy and hereditary succession
themes.summary: Monarchy is attacked from two directions, nature and scripture. Kings came into the world like some new species exalted above their equals; the Jews asked for one against God’s will; hereditary succession hands nations to fools and minors and has caused more civil wars than it has prevented. The English king has little to do but make war and give away places, and is paid eight hundred thousand pounds a year for it. In America, Paine says, the law is king.
themes.development: Male and female are the distinctions of nature; an ass for a lion; a French bastard with an armed banditti; crowned ruffians; the Royal Brute of Britain; in America the law is king.

themes.name: Society and government
themes.summary: The pamphlet opens with a distinction that became famous: society is produced by our wants and government by our wickedness, so that government at best is a necessary evil. Paine’s ideal is simple, representative and often elected, and he mocks the celebrated balance of the English constitution as a machine in which the crown, holding the key, always has its way. His plan for a continental charter, with a large and equal representation, is offered only as hints for something better.
themes.development: Society is produced by our wants; the colony under a tree; the key given to the crown; a Continental Charter; virtue is not hereditary.

themes.name: Nature and reason
themes.summary: Against custom and authority, Paine appeals to nature and common sense. Nature disapproves of hereditary right, has placed England and America in different systems, and has deserted the connection; the simple voice of nature and of reason will say what is right. The title itself claims that the argument needs no learning to follow.
themes.development: Time makes more converts than reason; the simple voice of nature and of reason; nature disapproves it; Nature hath deserted the connexion.

themes.name: Union
themes.summary: From the seed time of continental union in Common Sense to the last Supernumerary Crisis, Paine argues that American strength lies in unity. The thirteenth Crisis calls the union of the states the great hinge on which the whole machine turned and the most sacred thing in the constitution of America, and the final paper warns that the states, separated, are a medley of individual nothings.
themes.development: It is not in numbers, but in unity, that our great strength lies; the union, that great palladium of our liberty and safety; Our great title is AMERICANS; a medley of individual nothings.

themes.name: Courage
themes.summary: The Crisis papers were written to keep an army and a public from giving up. Paine despises the summer soldier and the sunshine patriot, loves the man who can smile in trouble, and treats every setback, from the retreat across New Jersey to the loss of Charleston, as a test that will make the country firmer. What we obtain too cheap, he says, we esteem too lightly.
themes.development: These are the times that try men’s souls; I love the man that can smile in trouble; Those who expect to reap the blessings of freedom; America ever is what she thinks herself to be.

themes.name: Trade and peace
themes.summary: Paine’s America is a trading nation whose plan is commerce. Its corn will fetch its price in any market in Europe, the connection with Britain only drags it into European wars, and war can never be the interest of a trading nation. After the peace the same argument becomes a demand that the union be strong enough to protect American shipping.
themes.development: Our plan is commerce; the make-weight in the scale of British politics; a bull-dog set upon a customer; Lord Sheffield and the carrying trade.

themes.name: Scripture and conscience
themes.summary: Scripture supplies arguments against kings, from Gideon’s refusal of a crown to Samuel’s warning, and Paine calls monarchy the Popery of government. He asks government to protect all conscientious professors of religion and to do nothing more, likens the denominations to children of one family, and rebukes the Quaker leaders for mixing religion with politics.
themes.development: Gideon and Samuel; monarchy is the Popery of government; children of the same family; Call not coldness of soul, religion.

themes.name: Posterity
themes.summary: Common Sense constantly measures the present against the future. The least fracture in the union will grow like a name cut into a young oak, a patched-up peace would leave the sword to our children, and a parent who wants peace in his own day wrongs his child. Paine asks his readers to take their children in their hand and look a few years further into life.
themes.development: posterity read it in full grown characters; leaving the sword to our children; let it be in my day, that my child may have peace; an inheritance for posterity.

themes.name: Whig and Tory
themes.summary: Paine writes as a partisan of the Whigs, who supported independence, against the Tories who stayed loyal to the Crown. Common Sense hopes that the two names will be extinct. The Crisis papers, written in a war in which loyalists fought beside the British, grow harsher, calling every Tory a coward and proposing tests of allegiance, taxes and exile for the disaffected.
themes.development: Let the names of Whig and Tory be extinct; Every Tory is a coward; Here is the touchstone to try men by; the warm passions of a Whig and the cold malice of a Tory.

techniques.name: Plain style
techniques.definition: Short, direct sentences in everyday words, written for readers without learning.
techniques.inThisBook: Common Sense promises nothing more than simple facts, plain arguments and common sense, and Paine writes for tradesmen and farmers as much as for lawyers. His images come from ordinary life, last year’s almanac, an apprentice nearly out of his time, a man putting off unpleasant business, and his paragraphs often end on a blunt verdict: A mere absurdity! Reconciliation and ruin are nearly related. Edmund Randolph, who served on Washington’s staff, later said that no one on this side of the Atlantic had written in such a style before.

techniques.name: Direct address
techniques.definition: A narrator or speaker turning outward to address the reader or the audience by name.
techniques.inThisBook: Readers and enemies alike are spoken to directly: ye that love mankind, ye that tell us of harmony and reconciliation, your lordship, sir. Most of the Crisis papers are open letters, to Lord Howe, Sir William Howe, the British commissioners, the people of England and Lord Shelburne, printed in American newspapers and sent, as Paine says, to England too.

techniques.name: Antithesis
techniques.definition: Opposed ideas set against each other in balanced phrases.
techniques.inThisBook: Pairs organise Paine’s thinking: society and government, wants and wickedness, a blessing and a necessary evil, the king as law and the law as king. The Crisis opens with the summer soldier and the sunshine patriot, and closes the war by turning the times that try men’s souls into the times that tried them.

techniques.name: Epigram
techniques.definition: A short balanced sentence that sounds like settled wisdom and usually turns a received idea inside out.
techniques.inThisBook: Many of Paine’s sentences were built to be remembered and repeated: Time makes more converts than reason; the cause of America is in a great measure the cause of all mankind; These are the times that try men’s souls; America ever is what she thinks herself to be.

techniques.name: Analogy
techniques.definition: Reasoning from a familiar case to an unfamiliar one.
techniques.inThisBook: Homely comparisons carry many of the arguments: a child that has thrived on milk will still need meat, no satellite is larger than its planet, a guardian who has grown rich on his ward resents his coming of age, and making war on your customers is like setting a bull-dog upon one at the shop door.

techniques.name: Rhetorical questions
techniques.definition: Questions asked for effect, where the answer is assumed.
techniques.inThisBook: Common Sense asks the reconciler: Hath your house been burnt? Hath your property been destroyed before your face? Anyone who can still shake hands with the murderers has the heart of a coward. The Crisis papers use questions to corner their addressees, asking Lord Howe what powers he means, when as a commissioner he has none.

techniques.name: Objection and reply
techniques.definition: Stating an opponent’s argument in order to answer it.
techniques.inThisBook: Much of Common Sense is a series of objections answered: But she has protected us, say some; But Britain is the parent country, say some; But where says some is the King of America? Paine gives the opposing case in its plainest form and disposes of it in the next sentence.

techniques.name: Argument from scripture
techniques.definition: Appealing to the Bible as an authority in a political argument.
techniques.inThisBook: Writing for Bible readers, Paine turns scripture against kings. He retells Gideon’s refusal of a crown and Samuel’s warning of what a king would take, quoting the prophet at length, and calls on Pharaoh, Mammon and the Popery of government. The address to the Quakers meets their Testimony on its own religious ground.

techniques.name: Invective
techniques.definition: Sustained personal abuse used as argument.
techniques.inThisBook: Paine can be ferocious: the Royal Brute of Britain, the sullen-tempered Pharaoh of England, a sottish, stupid, stubborn, worthless, brutish man. The fifth Crisis is an extended mock design for Sir William Howe’s monument. Paine’s defence, in the second Crisis, is that words were made for use, and the fault lies in deserving them.

techniques.name: Figures and accounts
techniques.definition: Arguing with numbers, tables and costs.
techniques.inThisBook: Arithmetic backs the rhetoric. The enlarged Common Sense adds a table of the cost of building warships of every rate to show that America could afford a navy, and the Crisis Extraordinary sets British taxes of about forty shillings a head against the thirteen shillings and fourpence a head that would defend and govern America.

quotations.text: a long habit of not thinking a thing wrong, gives it a superficial appearance of being right, and raises at first a formidable outcry in defense of custom. But the tumult soon subsides. Time makes more converts than reason.
quotations.context: The opening paragraph of the pamphlet, which warns that its ideas may not yet be fashionable.
quotations.analysis: Before arguing anything, Paine explains why his readers may resist him: habit makes the familiar feel right. The paragraph gives the reader permission to change his mind, and its last sentence, a short epigram after a long one, predicts that time will do the rest.
quotations.source: Common Sense, Bradford edition, 1776, Introduction

quotations.text: The cause of America is in a great measure the cause of all mankind.
quotations.context: In the Introduction Paine explains why the quarrel concerns every lover of mankind, and why he has left out anything personal.
quotations.analysis: A dispute over taxes and charters becomes a question for the whole world. The claim flatters American readers and lets anyone, from anywhere, claim a stake in the outcome. It also sets up the pamphlet’s later vision of America as an asylum for mankind.
quotations.source: Common Sense, Bradford edition, 1776, Introduction

quotations.text: Society is produced by our wants, and government by our wickedness; the former promotes our happiness positively by uniting our affections, the latter negatively by restraining our vices.
quotations.reference: Common Sense, Of the Origin and Design of Government
quotations.context: The opening of the first section, after Paine complains that some writers confuse society with government.
quotations.analysis: Everything in the sentence comes in pairs: society and government, wants and wickedness, positively and negatively. The balance makes a radical idea sound like common sense, since government is a remedy for our faults and nothing grander. A people can therefore change its government without losing its society.
quotations.source: Common Sense, Bradford edition, 1776, Of the Origin and Design of Government

quotations.text: Government, like dress, is the badge of lost innocence; the palaces of kings are built on the ruins of the bowers of paradise.
quotations.reference: Common Sense, Of the Origin and Design of Government
quotations.context: Society in every state is a blessing, Paine has just said, but government even in its best state is a necessary evil.
quotations.analysis: Clothing became necessary after the Fall, and so did government. The second half of the sentence moves from Genesis to politics: royal palaces stand where paradise once was. Readers who knew their Bible would feel the argument before they had followed it.
quotations.source: Common Sense, Bradford edition, 1776, Of the Origin and Design of Government

quotations.text: Some convenient tree will afford them a State-House, under the branches of which, the whole colony may assemble to deliberate on public matters.
quotations.reference: Common Sense, Of the Origin and Design of Government
quotations.context: A small group of settlers, imagined in some sequestered part of the earth, is driven into society by need.
quotations.analysis: Politics begins out of doors, with every man holding a seat by natural right. Paine then shows representation growing as the colony grows, with frequent elections to keep the members honest. For readers in Philadelphia, whose own State House was the seat of Congress, the tree was a pointed image.
quotations.source: Common Sense, Bradford edition, 1776, Of the Origin and Design of Government

quotations.text: though we have been wise enough to shut and lock a door against absolute monarchy, we at the same time have been foolish enough to put the crown in possession of the key.
quotations.reference: Common Sense, Of the Origin and Design of Government
quotations.context: Earlier in the section the crown, as the giver of places and pensions, is shown to be the overbearing part of the English constitution.
quotations.analysis: Here a whole theory of the balanced constitution is reduced to a domestic image anyone could understand. The English boasted that they had locked out absolute monarchy; Paine replies that the king keeps the key, because he controls the offices that buy the Commons.
quotations.source: Common Sense, Bradford edition, 1776, Of the Origin and Design of Government

quotations.text: Male and female are the distinctions of nature, good and bad the distinctions of heaven; but how a race of men came into the world so exalted above the rest, and distinguished like some new species, is worth enquiring into,
quotations.reference: Common Sense, Of Monarchy and Hereditary Succession
quotations.context: Differences of wealth, Paine has just said, can be explained without appeal to oppression.
quotations.analysis: Two natural distinctions are granted so that a third can be questioned. Calling kings a new species makes monarchy look absurd, a biological oddity, and the mild phrase is worth enquiring into makes the attack sound like simple curiosity.
quotations.source: Common Sense, Bradford edition, 1776, Of Monarchy and Hereditary Succession

quotations.text: One of the strongest natural proofs of the folly of hereditary right in kings, is, that nature disapproves it, otherwise she would not so frequently turn it into ridicule by giving mankind an ass for a lion.
quotations.reference: Common Sense, Of Monarchy and Hereditary Succession
quotations.context: Having dealt with monarchy itself, Paine turns to hereditary succession, which he calls an insult and an imposition on posterity.
quotations.analysis: Nature becomes a satirist, mocking the principle of inheritance every time a great king is followed by a fool. The lion is the traditional royal beast, and the ass its comic opposite. Later in the section Paine invites anyone who still believes in hereditary right to worship the ass and lion together.
quotations.source: Common Sense, Bradford edition, 1776, Of Monarchy and Hereditary Succession

quotations.text: In the following pages I offer nothing more than simple facts, plain arguments, and common sense;
quotations.reference: Common Sense, Thoughts on the Present State of American Affairs
quotations.context: The opening of the third section, the heart of the pamphlet.
quotations.analysis: Method and title are named together in one modest phrase. The claim to plainness is itself a strategy: it sets the reader’s own judgement against the learned arguments of lawyers and ministers, and asks him to divest himself of prejudice before reading on.
quotations.source: Common Sense, Bradford edition, 1776, Thoughts on the Present State of American Affairs

quotations.text: Now is the seed time of continental union, faith and honor. The least fracture now will be like a name engraved with the point of a pin on the tender rind of a young oak; the wound will enlarge with the tree, and posterity read it in full grown characters.
quotations.reference: Common Sense, Thoughts on the Present State of American Affairs
quotations.context: Just before this, Paine has written that the sun never shined on a cause of greater worth.
quotations.analysis: Rural readers would know that a mark scratched on a sapling grows with it. The image makes a political choice a matter of timing: whatever is done now will be magnified for generations. It also makes posterity the judge of the present.
quotations.source: Common Sense, Bradford edition, 1776, Thoughts on the Present State of American Affairs

quotations.text: Europe, and not England, is the parent country of America. This new world hath been the asylum for the persecuted lovers of civil and religious liberty from every part of Europe.
quotations.reference: Common Sense, Thoughts on the Present State of American Affairs
quotations.context: To those who say that Britain is the parent country, Paine replies: then the more shame upon her conduct.
quotations.analysis: By widening the family, Paine takes the emotional force out of the phrase mother country. Not one third of Pennsylvanians, he points out, are of English descent, and in his version the first settlers fled the cruelty of a monster.
quotations.source: Common Sense, Bradford edition, 1776, Thoughts on the Present State of American Affairs

quotations.text: Every thing that is right or natural pleads for separation. The blood of the slain, the weeping voice of nature cries, 'Tis time to part.
quotations.reference: Common Sense, Thoughts on the Present State of American Affairs
quotations.context: Every European war, Paine has argued, drags America in while she depends on Britain.
quotations.analysis: After pages of reasoning about trade and war, Paine lets feeling speak. Nature and the dead of Lexington and Bunker Hill share one voice, and the sentence ends on a phrase as simple as a parting between people. He goes on to argue that even the distance between the two countries shows Heaven never meant one to rule the other.
quotations.source: Common Sense, Bradford edition, 1776, Thoughts on the Present State of American Affairs

quotations.text: Small islands not capable of protecting themselves, are the proper objects for kingdoms to take under their care; but there is something very absurd, in supposing a continent to be perpetually governed by an island.
quotations.reference: Common Sense, Thoughts on the Present State of American Affairs
quotations.context: Britain, Paine argues, is too distant and too ignorant of America to govern it.
quotations.analysis: Geography becomes an argument. The next sentence adds astronomy: in no instance hath nature made the satellite larger than its primary planet. Paine’s appeal is to the reader’s sense of proportion, which he trusts more than any constitutional precedent.
quotations.source: Common Sense, Bradford edition, 1776, Thoughts on the Present State of American Affairs

quotations.text: For as in absolute governments the King is law, so in free countries the law ought to be King; and there ought to be no other.
quotations.reference: Common Sense, Thoughts on the Present State of American Affairs
quotations.context: Where, says some, is the King of America? Paine answers that he reigns above, and proposes a ceremony for proclaiming a continental charter.
quotations.analysis: Reversing two words, Paine reverses a whole order of government. He even allows a crown to be placed on the charter for the ceremony, then orders it demolished and scattered among the people whose right it is.
quotations.source: Common Sense, Bradford edition, 1776, Thoughts on the Present State of American Affairs

quotations.text: Freedom hath been hunted round the globe. Asia, and Africa, have long expelled her--Europe regards her like a stranger, and England hath given her warning to depart. O! receive the fugitive, and prepare in time an asylum for mankind.
quotations.reference: Common Sense, Thoughts on the Present State of American Affairs
quotations.context: The close of the third section, which calls on all who love mankind to stand forth against the tyrant as well as the tyranny.
quotations.analysis: Freedom is personified as a refugee turned away from every continent, and England as a landlord giving her notice to quit. The appeal casts Americans as the hosts of a homeless guest. It is one of the pamphlet’s most quoted passages, and it returns to the claim that America’s cause belongs to all mankind.
quotations.source: Common Sense, Bradford edition, 1776, Thoughts on the Present State of American Affairs

quotations.text: I look on the various denominations among us, to be like children of the same family, differing only, in what is called, their Christian names.
quotations.reference: Common Sense, Of the Present Ability of America
quotations.context: Government, Paine says, has no business with religion except to protect all conscientious professors of it.
quotations.analysis: A pun carries the argument. Denominations differ as brothers’ Christian names differ, while they share the family name. Paine believes diversity of religious opinion is the will of the Almighty, a larger field for Christian kindness, and a continental government must protect it.
quotations.source: Common Sense, Bradford edition, 1776, Of the Present Ability of America

quotations.text: We have it in our power to begin the world over again. A situation, similar to the present, hath not happened since the days of Noah until now. The birthday of a new world is at hand,
quotations.context: Near the end of the Appendix, Paine says that an independence brought about by the legal voice of the people in Congress could produce the noblest, purest constitution on earth.
quotations.analysis: This is the pamphlet at its most visionary. The comparison with Noah makes the present moment a second beginning after a flood, and the birthday of a new world gives it the hope of a birth. In the next sentences Paine sets ‘a race of men, perhaps as numerous as all Europe contains’ against the ‘little, paltry cavellings’ of ‘a few weak or interested men’.
quotations.source: Common Sense, Bradford edition, 1776, Appendix

quotations.text: Call not coldness of soul, religion; nor put the Bigot in the place of the Christian.
quotations.context: Addressing the authors of the Quaker Testimony, Paine says that Americans are defending their homes against highwaymen and housebreakers.
quotations.analysis: Paine, whose father was a Quaker, turns the Friends’ own principles against the Testimony’s authors. He accuses them of mistaking a lack of feeling for the sufferers in America for piety, and, a little later, of having mistaken party for conscience.
quotations.source: Common Sense, Bradford edition, 1776, To the Quakers

quotations.text: These are the times that try men's souls. The summer soldier and the sunshine patriot will, in this crisis, shrink from the service of their country; but he that stands it now, deserves the love and thanks of man and woman.
quotations.context: The opening of the first Crisis, printed on 19 December 1776, after the army had retreated across New Jersey to the Delaware.
quotations.analysis: Alliteration does much of the work: summer soldier and sunshine patriot are volunteers who serve only in fair weather. The first sentence was short enough to become a watchword, and the next lines add that what we obtain too cheap, we esteem too lightly. According to tradition, Washington had the paper read to his troops before Trenton.
quotations.source: The American Crisis, ed. Conway, Crisis I

quotations.text: a generous parent should have said, "If there must be trouble, let it be in my day, that my child may have peace;"
quotations.context: A Tory tavern-keeper at Amboy, standing at his door with a child by the hand, had ended a conversation with Well! give me peace in my day.
quotations.analysis: Through a remembered scene, Paine answers a whole political attitude. The tavern-keeper wants the trouble postponed; Paine rewrites his words so that a parent takes the danger on himself to spare his child. This single reflection, he says, is enough to awaken every man to duty.
quotations.source: The American Crisis, ed. Conway, Crisis I

quotations.text: Your lordship, I find, has now commenced author, and published a proclamation; I have published a Crisis.
quotations.context: Lord Howe had issued a proclamation offering pardon to those who abandoned the Congress; this is Paine’s reply of January 1777.
quotations.analysis: Paine treats the proclamation as a rival piece of writing and himself as Howe’s equal. The joke carries a serious claim from the paper’s first sentence, that universal empire is the prerogative of a writer, and that argument can answer power.
quotations.source: The American Crisis, ed. Conway, Crisis II

quotations.text: Britain was too jealous of America to govern it justly; too ignorant of it to govern it well; and too far distant from it to govern it at all.
quotations.context: Even without a war, the third Crisis argues, independence would soon have come.
quotations.analysis: Three clauses, each harsher than the last, run from justly to well to at all. The rhythm makes a complex historical judgement feel settled. Jealousy, ignorance and distance repeat the arguments of Common Sense in a single sentence.
quotations.source: The American Crisis, ed. Conway, Crisis III

quotations.text: Those who expect to reap the blessings of freedom, must, like men, undergo the fatigues of supporting it.
quotations.context: The opening of the fourth Crisis, dated 12 September 1777, the day after the defeat at the Brandywine.
quotations.analysis: Freedom is described as a harvest that must be worked for. Written with the enemy advancing on Philadelphia, the paper treats the defeat as an alarm just sufficient to rouse us to duty, and reminds readers that what they are defending is a cause, whatever happens to a few acres of ground.
quotations.source: The American Crisis, ed. Conway, Crisis IV

quotations.text: the grave is nevertheless a perfect republic. Death is not the monarch of the dead, but of the dying.
quotations.context: In the fifth Crisis Paine considers, with mock seriousness, what funeral honours would suit Sir William Howe.
quotations.analysis: In the middle of a satirical address to Howe, Paine finds a republican truth: in death all are equal. The second sentence adds a paradox, and then applies it to George III, who, like Death, loses a subject with every conquest and will war himself out of his dominions.
quotations.source: The American Crisis, ed. Conway, Crisis V

quotations.text: There is a dignity in the warm passions of a Whig, which is never to be found in the cold malice of a Tory.
quotations.context: The opening of the sixth Crisis, addressed to the British peace commissioners in October 1778.
quotations.analysis: Warm and cold divide the two parties as clearly as virtue and vice. In the next sentences nature is only heated in the Whig and poisoned in the Tory, and the Whig forgives while the Tory can only revenge. Paine applies the distinction to England as well as America.
quotations.source: The American Crisis, ed. Conway, Crisis VI

quotations.text: War never can be the interest of a trading nation, any more than quarrelling can be profitable to a man in business. But to make war with those who trade with us, is like setting a bull-dog upon a customer at the shop-door.
quotations.context: Addressing the people of England in November 1778, Paine asks what, in the name of heaven, Britain went to war for.
quotations.analysis: The English are spoken to as shopkeepers, in the language of their own interest. The first sentence is a principle, the second a comic picture of it. America was Britain’s customer, and the war attacks the trade it was meant to secure.
quotations.source: The American Crisis, ed. Conway, Crisis VII

quotations.text: For in a country where all men were once adventurers, the difference of a few years in their arrival could make none in their right.
quotations.context: Recalling his arrival in America, Paine says that when the country was set on fire about his ears, it was time to stir.
quotations.analysis: Paine had arrived only months before the fighting began, and here he claims the same right to take part as anyone born in America. The sentence makes immigration the country’s founding condition, and gives the latest arrival the same right as the first settler.
quotations.source: The American Crisis, ed. Conway, Crisis VII

quotations.text: Like fire at a distance you heard not even the cry; you felt not the danger, you saw not the confusion. To you every thing has been foreign but the taxes to support it.
quotations.context: Writing to the people of England in March 1780, Paine says that they have known the expenses of the war but nothing of its miseries.
quotations.analysis: Paine makes the English feel their own safety as a moral failing. The repeated not builds a list of things they have been spared, and the last clause turns on one exception, taxes. With French and Spanish fleets in the Channel and John Paul Jones on their coasts, he warns, they may soon learn what invasion means.
quotations.source: The American Crisis, ed. Conway, Crisis VIII

quotations.text: America ever is what she thinks herself to be.
quotations.context: In June 1780 the loss of Charleston had been reported, and Paine hopes the news will rouse the country from a year’s slumber.
quotations.analysis: Morale, in this sentence, is destiny: governed by sentiment, America becomes, as she pleases, the victor or the victim. The idea runs through all the Crisis papers, which exist to change what the country thinks of itself.
quotations.source: The American Crisis, ed. Conway, Crisis IX

quotations.text: even the light from heaven is only permitted to shine into their dwellings by paying eighteen pence sterling per window annually;
quotations.context: Here the Crisis Extraordinary lists what Americans would pay if Britain conquered them and taxed them as heavily as the English.
quotations.analysis: After pages of figures, Paine gives the reader one image to remember: a tax on daylight. The window tax, like the duties on rum, coffee and small beer he also lists, makes the abstract sum of six millions a year into a daily burden in every house.
quotations.source: The American Crisis, ed. Conway, Crisis Extraordinary

quotations.text: I consider the war of America against Britain as the country's war, the public's war, or the war of the people in their own behalf,
quotations.context: In the address to the people of America in the tenth Crisis, written after Yorktown, Paine turns to the quotas Congress has asked the states to pay.
quotations.analysis: Paine repeats the word war to insist on whose it is. If the war belongs to the people, and not to Congress or the assemblies, then paying for it is every citizen’s obligation. It is a political argument for taxation made in the name of popular sovereignty.
quotations.source: The American Crisis, ed. Conway, Crisis X

quotations.text: give up the murderer, and save your officer, as the first outset of a necessary reformation.
quotations.context: The last words of Paine’s letter of May 1782 about the hanging of Captain Huddy and the retaliation threatened against Captain Asgill.
quotations.analysis: Paine reduces a painful case to a plain choice for Carleton: surrender the loyalist Lippincott, or be responsible for the death of an innocent British captain. The letter separates the villain from the victim, and puts the decision squarely on the British commander.
quotations.source: The American Crisis, ed. Conway, Supernumerary Crisis

quotations.text: Was America, then, the giant of the empire, and England only her dwarf in waiting!
quotations.context: Lord Shelburne had said that the sun of England’s glory would set with American independence.
quotations.analysis: The opponent’s gloomy prophecy is read as a confession. If England cannot shine without America, then America was the true giant all along. The joke borrows a figure that Wedderburn had used in 1776, of a giant asked to shrink into a dwarf.
quotations.source: The American Crisis, ed. Conway, Crisis XII

quotations.text: "The times that tried men's souls," are over--and the greatest and completest revolution the world ever knew, gloriously and happily accomplished.
quotations.context: The opening of the thirteenth Crisis, dated 19 April 1783, eight years after the fighting at Lexington.
quotations.analysis: Quoting himself, Paine changes one tense. The series that began in the depth of winter ends with peace, and the change from try to tried gives a sense of completion. He goes on to warn that calm can stun as much as a storm.
quotations.source: The American Crisis, ed. Conway, Crisis XIII

quotations.text: Our citizenship in the United States is our national character. Our citizenship in any particular state is only our local distinction. By the latter we are known at home, by the former to the world. Our great title is AMERICANS--our inferior one varies with the place.
quotations.context: Just before this passage, the union of the states is called the great palladium of liberty and safety, and Paine says he is hurt to hear it irreverently spoken of.
quotations.analysis: Written years before the Constitution, the passage argues that national citizenship must come first. The paired sentences set local against national, home against the world, and end on a single capitalised word. Paine is warning a loose confederation that it will be respected abroad only as one people.
quotations.source: The American Crisis, ed. Conway, Crisis XIII

quotations.text: It was the cause of America that made me an author.
quotations.context: Taking his leave of the subject, Paine says he has avoided all places of profit and all party connections.
quotations.analysis: Here Paine presents his whole career as a writer as a product of the Revolution. The sentence is modest and proud together: he claims no talent before the crisis called it out, and also that he has shown there may be genius without prostitution.
quotations.source: The American Crisis, ed. Conway, Crisis XIII

quotations.text: United, she is formidable, and that with the least possible charge a nation can be so; separated, she is a medley of individual nothings, subject to the sport of foreign nations.
quotations.reference: Supernumerary Crisis (To the People of America)
quotations.context: In December 1783 Paine answers Lord Sheffield, who had written that it would be a long time before the American states could act as a nation.
quotations.analysis: United and separated open the two halves of the sentence, and the second half collapses into a medley of individual nothings. The occasion is British restrictions on American shipping, but the lesson is the need for a stronger union, which Paine thinks the states’ quarrels over an import duty have shown to the world.
quotations.source: The American Crisis, ed. Conway, Supernumerary Crisis

timeline.label: Thomas Paine is born
timeline.detail: On 29 January (1736 in the old reckoning), at Thetford in Norfolk, the son of a Quaker staymaker.

timeline.label: Paine reaches Philadelphia
timeline.detail: Dismissed from the excise, Paine sails for America with a letter of introduction from Benjamin Franklin and arrives on 30 November.

timeline.label: Lexington and Concord
timeline.detail: The first fighting of the war, on 19 April, which Paine says ended any hope of reconciliation.

timeline.label: Common Sense
timeline.detail: Published by Robert Bell in Philadelphia on 10 January, without the author’s name; the enlarged Bradford edition follows on 14 February.

timeline.label: The Declaration of Independence
timeline.detail: Congress adopts the Declaration on 4 July.

timeline.label: The first Crisis
timeline.detail: Begun at Newark during the retreat across New Jersey and printed in the Pennsylvania Journal on 19 December, a week before Trenton.

timeline.label: Secretary for foreign affairs
timeline.detail: On 17 April Congress elects Paine secretary to its Committee of Foreign Affairs. He resigns on 8 January 1779 after his public attack on Silas Deane.

timeline.label: The Crisis Extraordinary
timeline.detail: Published on 4 October, it argues that Americans pay a fraction of the taxes the English pay and must fund the war.

timeline.label: Mission to France
timeline.detail: Paine sails from Boston in February with John Laurens to seek French money, and returns from Brest in June.

timeline.label: The last Crisis
timeline.detail: The thirteenth paper appears on 19 April, eight years after Lexington, and a Supernumerary Crisis follows from New York on 9 December.

timeline.label: Rights of Man
timeline.detail: Paine publishes the first part in London in 1791 and the second in February 1792, and is elected to the French National Convention.

timeline.label: The Luxembourg prison
timeline.detail: On 28 December Paine is imprisoned in Paris during the Terror.

timeline.label: Paine dies
timeline.detail: On 8 June, at Greenwich village in New York.

places.name: Philadelphia
places.note: Where Common Sense was printed in 1776, and where most of the Crisis papers were written and published.

places.name: Fort Lee, New Jersey
places.note: The garrison on the Hudson where the retreat of November 1776 began.

places.name: Newark, New Jersey
places.note: Where Paine began the first Crisis during the retreat.

places.name: Trenton, New Jersey
places.note: Where Washington’s army won its victory on 26 December 1776, a week after the first Crisis appeared.

places.name: Lancaster, Pennsylvania
places.note: Where Paine dated the fifth Crisis in March 1778, while the British held Philadelphia.

criticalViews.summary: Contemporaries credited Common Sense with turning American opinion towards independence in the first half of 1776. Washington wrote of its sound doctrine and unanswerable reasoning, Benjamin Rush of an effect rarely produced by types and paper, and Paine claimed sales of 120,000 copies in three months.
criticalViews.counter: The sales figure is Paine’s own estimate, and the pamphlet appeared when events were pushing the same way: Washington paired it with the burning of Falmouth and Norfolk, and the king’s hostile speech arrived on the day of publication.

criticalViews.summary: Many readers have seen Paine’s real revolution in his prose. He wrote for ordinary readers, without Latin or legal learning, in short sentences and homely images, and treated them as judges of the question. The style itself assumes that political argument belongs to everyone.
criticalViews.counter: Opponents such as Plain Truth, printed by the same Robert Bell in 1776, argued that the scheme of independence was ruinous, delusive and impracticable, and Paine’s simplicity can flatten real difficulties, as the harder arguments of the later Crisis papers about taxes and union suggest.

criticalViews.summary: The Crisis papers can be read as wartime propaganda, written to raise morale, shame the wavering and answer British proclamations as they appeared.
criticalViews.counter: They are also a sustained argument about what the new country needed: a sense of national character, taxes paid to a common fund, and a union strong enough to deal with other nations. The last papers look forward to the debates that produced the Constitution.

essayQuestions.question: How does Paine persuade his readers that independence is common sense?
essayQuestions.focus: Argument, style and audience in Common Sense
plan: Begin with the title and the opening paragraph on habit, custom and reason.
Analyse the distinction between society and government, and the attack on the English constitution.
Examine the arguments against monarchy and hereditary succession, including scripture.
Discuss objection and reply in the answers to the reconcilers, and the use of analogy.
Conclude on the plain style as itself an argument.

essayQuestions.question: How do the Crisis papers try to sustain the American cause through a long war?
essayQuestions.focus: Courage, shame and reasoning in The American Crisis
plan: Start with the first Crisis: the summer soldier, the retreat and the tavern-keeper at Amboy.
Consider the open letters to Lord Howe, Sir William Howe and the commissioners.
Examine the appeals to the people of England and the arguments about trade.
Discuss the Crisis Extraordinary and the tenth Crisis on taxes and quotas.
Conclude with the thirteenth Crisis and the union of the states.

essayQuestions.question: How does Paine present monarchy and the British government in these writings?
plan: Examine the scriptural and historical case against kings in Common Sense.
Analyse the images: the lock and key, the ass for a lion, the Royal Brute of Britain.
Consider the Appendix on the king’s speech.
Discuss the later Crisis papers’ treatment of British ministers and generals.
Assess how far invective strengthens or weakens the argument.

discussionQuestions: Why might Paine have published Common Sense without his name?
Which of Paine’s analogies is most persuasive, and which least?
Is government really, as Paine says, a necessary evil?
How does the tone of the Crisis papers change between 1776 and 1783?
Should an argument about politics use personal abuse, as Paine often does?
What does Paine mean by calling the union of the states the most sacred thing in the constitution of America?
